Why Agile Post-Quantum Cryptography Matters for Long-Lived Chip Designsby Daniel Nenni on 11-17-2026 at 8:00 am

View Profile

View Forum Posts

View Articles

Private Message

Categories: EDA, Quantum Computing, Security, Synopsys

Key takeaways ▼

Quantum computing opens exciting possibilities for solving difficult problems, advancing research, and enabling new technologies. Preparing security for that future is an opportunity to strengthen the digital foundations supporting everyday life. Synopsys’ Agile PQC Public Key Accelerators offer chip designers a practical starting point, combining hardware, firmware, and software to bring post-quantum cryptography into systems being developed today.
The opportunity is particularly meaningful for products expected to operate for many years. Vehicles, industrial equipment, networking infrastructure, and connected devices need security that can evolve throughout their service lives. By considering quantum resilience during chip development, manufacturers can create a stronger foundation for protecting information, authenticating software, and maintaining trust as computing capabilities advance.
The Synopsys portfolio supports several post-quantum algorithms with complementary roles. ML-KEM enables the establishment of shared secrets, while ML-DSA supports digital signatures. SLH-DSA, XMSS, and LMS provide hash-based signature options. Together, these capabilities give designers choices for addressing confidentiality and authenticity requirements across different applications, helping translate cryptographic standards into implementable system functions.
This matters because digital trust depends on more than keeping information private. Systems also need to verify that software updates come from authorized sources and that communications originate from legitimate participants. Post-quantum key establishment and signature capabilities can help designers prepare these essential functions for future threats. Building that readiness early supports more deliberate development and migration planning.
An encouraging aspect of the architecture is its support for established RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography alongside post-quantum algorithms. Organizations can therefore plan transitions while accommodating existing infrastructure and compatibility needs. That flexibility creates room for staged adoption, allowing engineering teams to introduce new capabilities as protocols, customer requirements, and deployment plans mature.
Agility is another central advantage. The datasheet describes a firmware-driven control engine that enables field updates to public-key algorithms, with firmware stored in RAM or ROM depending on the configuration. For implementations designed to support updates, this provides a path for adapting cryptographic functionality over time. The practical benefit depends on the chosen architecture and secure update mechanisms.
Configurability gives designers further room to match security capabilities to their products. Processing resources, storage, and firmware can be scaled to balance performance, power, and silicon area. A data-center application and an embedded controller have different priorities, making this flexibility valuable. Specific performance and area results remain configuration-dependent; the datasheet directs customers to Synopsys for benchmarks.
The offering also addresses the protection of cryptographic implementations. A secure private-key interface supports connections with external key-management resources, while optional countermeasures target differential power analysis, timing analysis, and fault injection. These features help designers consider how secrets are handled and how hardware behaves under attack, complementing the selection of suitable algorithms.
For automotive applications, the architecture extends into functional safety. The automotive variant includes redundancy, fault detection, diagnostic reporting, and safety monitoring. Its illustrated design incorporates main and shadow processing paths, output comparison, memory protection, and bus protection. These mechanisms support the broader engineering goal of building systems that remain dependable when hardware faults or abnormal conditions occur.
Integration support adds practical value. Deliverables include hardware design files, firmware, host software, testbench materials, synthesis guidance, and documentation. Automotive deliverables also include safety and cybersecurity assessment materials. These resources give development teams a more concrete basis for implementation and evaluation, helping them connect cryptographic capabilities with the requirements of their complete products.
Bottom line: Quantum readiness creates an opportunity to build durable confidence into tomorrow’s technology. Synopsys’ Agile PQC Public Key Accelerators bring together algorithm choice, configurable hardware, and adaptable control to support that goal. With careful integration and validation, designers can use these capabilities to prepare products for changing security requirements while continuing to deliver useful, connected experiences. The optimistic message is practical: engineering decisions made today can help tomorrow’s systems remain trustworthy, adaptable, and ready for progress across industries and throughout their working lives.
